segments.text: You used to see these names everywhere, on every street corner, in every mall, in every
American home.
Then one day they were gone, not bought, not merged, not renamed, gone.
Six brands that once defined America erased from existence, and the reasons why will
change how you look at every company you trust today.
At its peak, Blockbuster had 9,000 stores, 9,000.
Every Friday night, millions of mallies walked through those doors.
The blue and yellow sign was as American as apple pie, they made 5 billion dollars
a year just from renting plastic boxes.
In the year 2000, a small company came to Blockbuster with an offer, biased for
50 million dollars.
Blockbuster laughed, the company was Netflix, they didn't just say no, they laughed the
founders out of the room.
By 2010, Blockbuster filed for bankruptcy, every single store closed except one.
One Blockbuster remains in Benidorm, it's not a store anymore, it's a museum of
a company that refused to see the future.
The lesson is simple, it doesn't matter how big you are, if you ignore what's
coming, what's coming ignores you.
There was a time when every kid in America knew one sentence by heart, I don't want
to grow up, I'm a Toys R Us kid.
That jingle played in every living room for 30 years.
Toys R Us was not just a store, it was a kingdom, 700 stores across America.
The giraffe mascot Jeffrey was more famous than most CEOs.
Kids didn't ask to go shopping, they asked to go to Toys R Us.
So what killed the kingdom?
Debt.
In 2005, a group of private equity firms bought Toys R Us for 6.5 billion dollars,
they didn't buy it with their own money.
They loaded the company with debt and made the company pay for its own purchase.
Every year, Toys R Us had to pay 400 million dollars just in interest, 400 million that
couldn't go to better stores, 400 million that couldn't go to online sales, 400
million bleeding out every single year.
By 2017, the debt won.
Toys R Us filed for bankruptcy and closed every American store.
Jeffrey the giraffe walked out the door and never came back.
In the 1960s, flying Pan Am meant you had arrived.
Movie stars, presidents, diplomats.
They all flew Pan Am.
The airline was so iconic it appeared in 2001.
A space odyssey.
A film set 30 years in the future because no one could imagine a future without Pan
Am.
But fuel prices tripled in the 1970s.
Deregulation opened the skies to cheaper competitors.
And then came December 21st, 1988.
Pan Am flight 103.
A bomb exploded over Lockerbie, Scotland.
270 people died.
The airline never recovered from the fear.
Bookings collapsed.
In 1991, after 64 years of flight, Pan Am landed for the last time.
The airline that taught the world to fly could not save itself.
For over a century, one word meant photography.
Kodak.
They didn't just sell cameras, they sold memories.
Your parents' wedding.
Your first birthday.
Your graduation.
Chances are, every major moment in your family's history sits on Kodak Film.
At its peak, Kodak employed over 145,000 people.
They controlled 90% of the film market in America.
The headquarters in Rochester, New York was a city within a city.
And here is the part that will haunt you.
In 1915, a Kodak engineer named Steve Sasson built the first digital camera.
He showed it to the executives.
They told him to hide it.
They buried the invention that would have saved the company
because they were afraid it would kill their film business.
It killed their film business anyway.
Every competitor adopted digital.
Kodak watched and waited and hoped film would survive.
It didn't.
In 2012, Kodak filed for bankruptcy.
The company that invented the digital camera
was destroyed by the digital camera.
They had the future in their hands.
And they put it in a drawer.
There was a time when Sears was not just a store.
It was America.
For most of the 20th century, Sears was the largest retailer on earth.
They sold everything.
Clothes, tools, appliances, houses.
Yes, houses.
You could order an entire home from the Sears catalog
and they would ship it to your door in pieces.
Over 70,000 Sears kit homes were sold.
Some of them are still standing today.
Sears built the tallest building in the world, the Sears Tower.
They launched a credit card before most banks did.
They created all state insurance, Discover Card,
even helped start what became Prodigy, one of the first internet services.
Sears had every piece of the puzzle to become Amazon.
20 years before Amazon existed, a national catalog.
A logistics network, a trusted brand.
But they didn't build a website.
They didn't build a warehouse network.
They didn't build anything new.
Instead, a hedge fund manager named Eddie Lampert took control.
He didn't invest in the company.
He stripped it for parts.
He sold the land.
He sold the brands.
He extracted every dollar he could while the stores rotted.
In 2018, Sears filed for bankruptcy.
The company that could have been Amazon chose to be nothing.
Polaroid gave you something no other camera could.
Instant magic.
You pressed the button, the photo slid out,
and you watched your memory appear right before your eyes.
No lab, no waiting, no negatives.
Just you, the camera, and 60 seconds of pure anticipation.
Edwin Land founded Polaroid in 1937.
He was called the second Steve Jobs,
except Jobs called himself the second Edwin Land.
At its peak, Polaroid was worth $3 billion.
They were untouchable.
And then digital cameras arrived,
but Polaroid didn't die like Kodak, slowly and in denial.
Polaroid panicked.
They pivoted to everything.
Portable DVD players, flat screen TVs,
digital cameras with no film.
They abandoned the one thing that made them special,
the instant print.
By 2001, Polaroid filed for bankruptcy.
The name got sold, resold, and licensed to cheap electronics.
For years, the Polaroid brand appeared on products
that had nothing to do with photography.
The magic was gone.
And here's the irony.
Years later, Instagram launched with a Polaroid-shaped icon.
The entire aesthetic of modern social media
is built on what Polaroid invented.
The company died.
But the idea never did.
Six brands, six empires.
Every one of them believed they were too big to fail.
Blockbuster ignored the future.
Toys R Us was crushed by debt.
Pan Am was destroyed by tragedy and competition.
Kodak buried its own invention.
Sears had the blueprint for Amazon and burned it.
Polaroid abandoned what made it magic.
The pattern is always the same.
It's never the market that kills a giant.
It's the giant that kills itself.
And right now, somewhere a company
you use every single day is making the same mistake.
If this changed how you see the brands around you,
subscribe.
Because the next story might be about a company
you think will last forever.
